steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (missing an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose (has an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA’s bases are adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA’s bases are adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) (instead of thymine).

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is usually double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is typically single-stranded and can fold into various shapes (hairpins, loops).

4. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable—its deoxyribose and lack of the 2′-OH group make it less prone to hydrolysis.  
   • RNA is more reactive and less stable (the 2′-OH group can attack the backbone).

5. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits genetic information in cells and across generations.  
   • RNA plays multiple roles in gene expression and regulation, including:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA): control gene expression.

6. Location in cells  
   • DNA is mainly confined to the nucleus (in eukaryotes) and to the nucleoid region (in prokaryotes).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) but functions throughout the cell, including the cytoplasm.

In summary, DNA is the long-term, stable repository of genetic information, whereas RNA is more versatile and transient, carrying out the processes that read, translate and regulate that information.
